parole.testo: The "date" sense is denominal from תַּאֲרִיךְ (ta'aríkh), a loanword from an Arabic word originally corresponding to the Hebrew root י־ר־ח (y-r-k) / יָרֵחַ (yaréakh, “moon”).
From Arabic إبزيم (ʔibzīm).
From Arabic اِبْن (ibn).

Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, inspired by Arabic Arabic ادُب (“cultured, mannerly”). Ben-Yehuda speculates that Biblical Hebrew may once have possessed the same root, possibly reflected in the name אַדְבְּאֵל.
Borrowed from Arabic أَهْلًا (ʾahlan, “hello”).
Borrowed from Arabic أُفُق (ʔufuq).

parole.significato: only used in אחושרמוטה and a small number of derived vulgarisms.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic أَخُو (ʔaḵū, “brother of”). Cognate of Hebrew אֲחִי־.
Borrowed from Arabic أَخُو شَرْمُوطَة (ʔaḵū šarmūṭa, literally “brother of a whore”).
From Arabic أَحْلَى (ʔaḥlā), comparative of حُلْو (ḥulw, “sweet”).

Calque of Arabic كيفية. Blending of אֵיךְ (ékh, “how”) + ־וּת (-út, “-ness, -ity; a suffix forming nouns, especially abstract nouns”), similar to the coinage of Latin quālitās (from which English quality is derived).
From Arabic إخسا.

parole.significato: imam (one who leads the salat prayers in a mosque)
parole.testo: From Arabic إِمَام (ʔimām).

parole.significato: God willing, with the help of God
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic إِنْ شَاءَ ٱللَٰه (ʔin šāʔa llāh, literally “if God has willed [it]”).
Ultimately borrowed from Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr).
From Arabic اَلْكُحْل (al-kuḥl, “kohl”).

From Arabic إما لَ (ʾimmā lā), equivalent to إما (ʾimmā, “if even”) + لَ (lā, “not”) cognate with Hebrew לֹא (lo). Likely adapted to form the compound אִי ('i, “not having, not being”) + לְמַלֵּא (lemalé, “to fulfill”).
From Arabic اِنْتِفَاضَة (intifāḍa).

parole.significato: peach (soft juicy stone fruit of the peach tree, having yellow flesh, downy, red-tinted yellow skin, and a deeply sculp…
parole.testo: From Arabic اَلفِرْسِك (al-firsik, “the peach”), from Ancient Greek περσικόν (persikón, “peach”), short for μῆλον Περσικόν (mêlon Persikón, “Persian apple”).

parole.significato: Climate, a climate: long-term atmospheric conditions in a region.
parole.testo: From Arabic إِقْلِيم (ʔiqlīm), from Ancient Greek κλίμα (klíma).
From Arabic بَأْسَاء (baʔsāʔ, “distress”).
Borrowed from Arabic بَابُونَج (bābūnaj), from Persian بابونه (bâbune). Compare Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܒܵܒ݂ܘܿܢܵܐ (bāḇōnā).

parole.significato: baharat: a Middle Eastern spice mixture
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic بَهَارَات (bahārāt).
Borrowed from Arabic بُول (būl, “postage stamp”). Compare Greek βούλα (voúla, “seal”), Latin bulla (“papal bull, seal”).
Borrowed from Arabic بُوسَة (būsa), from Classical Persian بوسَه (bōsa).
Borrowed from Arabic بُوقِيصَا (būqīṣā).

parole.significato: Traditional reply to בֹּקֶר טוֹב (bóker tov, “good morning”)
parole.testo: Calque of Arabic صَبَاح النُّور (ṣabāḥ an-nūr, literally “morning of light”).

parole.significato: A screw, a bolt: a threaded fastener.
parole.testo: Apparently adapted from Arabic بُرْغِيّ (burḡiyy, “screw, bolt”), ultimately from Ottoman Turkish بورغو (“drill; screw”).

parole.significato: to gibber, to babble, to chatter.
parole.testo: Likely borrowed from Arabic بَرْبَرَ (barbara, “to babble”).
Borrowed from Arabic جَوْرَب (jawrab).
Borrowed from Arabic قَات (qāt).
From Arabic جِهَاد (jihād, “struggle; effort”).

Ultimately from Arabic زَرَافَة (zarāfa), further etymology is disputed. Perhaps from Classical Persian زرناپا (zornâpâ, “giraffe”), a compound of زرنا (zornâ, “flute, zurna”) and پا (pâ, “leg”), or from Classical Syriac ܙܵܪܝܼܦܵܐ (zarāfa).
Borrowed from Arabic دَغْدَغَ (daḡdaḡa). It must be a relatively recent borrowing, as a more ancient cognate form would be *דִּעְדֵּעַ, given Arabic غ (along with ع) corresponds to ע and not ג.

parole.significato: Expressing incredulity: do me a favour
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic.

parole.significato: A type of goblet drum, originating in the Middle East and North Africa.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic دَرْبُوكَة (darbūka).

parole.significato: cardamom (Seed of Elettaria cardamomum, used as a medicine and spice, especially in curry powder)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic هَيْل (hayl), borrowed from Classical Persian هیل (hēl), borrowed from Sanskrit एला (elā), borrowed from a South Dravidian language, from Proto-South Dravidian *ēlV- (“cardamom”).
From Arabic هَنْدَسَة (handasa), from the same Iranic source as modern Persian اندازه (andâze, “measuring”).

parole.significato: to be Arabized, adopt Arab culture or language
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic اِسْتَعْرَبَ (istaʕraba).
Derived from Arabic شَهِيد (šahīd), literally "witness".
Borrowed from Arabic وَادِي (wādī).

parole.significato: an unrestrained, uncouth, rude, barbaric, wild person
parole.testo: From Arabic وَحْش (waḥš, “wild animal, beast”), via South Levantine Arabic.
Post-biblical Hebrew, borrowed at the latest by ancient medical practitioners from Arabic وَرِيد (warīd, “vein”).

parole.significato: no way, no chance, my ass, like hell
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic زِبِّي (zibbī), a dialectal variant of Arabic زُبِّي (zubbī, “no way”, literally “my cock”). Compare זַיִן שֶׁלִּי (záyin shelí), which is a calque of the same term.

parole.significato: no way, no chance, my ass, like hell
parole.testo: Calque of Arabic زُبِّي (zubbī, “no way”, literally “my cock”). Compare זיבי / זִבִּי (zíbi) and זובי / זֻבִּי (zúbi), which are direct loanwords from the same term.

parole.significato: to own; to defeat or embarrass; to overwhelm
parole.testo: Verb formed from the term זַמְבּוּרָה (zamburá, “car horn (slang)”), which is from Arabic زَمُّور (zammūr, “car horn”).

Medieval borrowing from Arabic زَنْجَبِيل (zanjabīl), and earlier still from Aramaic זַנְגְּבִילָא (zangḇīlā, zangəḇīlā) which is apart from various Babylonian Talmud Mishna Tractates notably found in the Targum Song of Songs 3:9 however the compilator of the TgSong is theoretized to be a native Ara
From Medieval Hebrew, from Arabic زَعْفَرَان (zaʕfarān).
From Arabic زَعْتَر (zaʕtar).
Borrowed from Arabic حَبِيبِي (ḥabībī); related to Hebrew חָבִיב (khavív, “friendly, pleasant; beloved; darling”, adjective and noun).

parole.significato: hajj (the pilgrimage to Mecca made by pious Muslims; the fifth of the five pillars of Islam)
parole.testo: From Arabic حَجّ (ḥajj). Cognate with native חַג (khág).

parole.significato: hummus (a Levantine Arab dip made of chickpea paste with various additions, such as olive oil, fresh garlic, lemon juic…
parole.testo: From Arabic حُمُّص (ḥummuṣ, “chickpea; hummus”).

parole.significato: A hijab, a headscarf: a traditional headscarf worn by Muslim women, covering the hair and neck.
parole.testo: From Arabic حِجَاب (ḥijāb, “veil”).
From Arabic حِنَّاء (ḥinnāʔ).

parole.significato: halva (a confection usually made from crushed sesame seeds and honey)
parole.testo: From Arabic حَلْوَى (ḥalwā).
From Arabic حَمَّام (ḥammām).

parole.significato: One with access to great knowledge, or who has such knowledge, but does not make use of it.
parole.testo: Literally, “a jackass carrying books”. Calque of Arabic كَمَثَلِ ٱلْحِمَارِ يَحْمِلُ أَسْفَارًا (kamaṯali l-ḥimāri yaḥmilu ʔasfāran) (Qur'an 62:5).

parole.significato: the Hand of Fatima, the hamsa amulet
parole.testo: From Arabic خَمْسَة (ḵamsa, “five”), for the five fingers on the hand.
Coined by Abraham Lunz in 1831, adapted from Arabic حَيْصَل (ḥayṣal).

parole.significato: to cause failure, to ruin, to spoil, to fuck something up
parole.testo: Back-formation from חֶרְבּוֹן (kherbón, “failure, disaster”), which is a phono-semantic matching of Arabic خَرْبَان (ḵarbān, “broken, damaged, spoiled”), and a doublet of חֻרְבָּן /חורבן (khurbán, “destruction, ruin”) and חֲרָבוֹן (kharavón, “drought, heat”).
Coined by Aharon Meir Mazya for a 1910 lecture on meningitis, based on the Arabic طُفَيْل (ṭufayl).
Borrowed from Arabic يَا (yā)

parole.significato: Vocative particle preceding a noun, especially a slur or pejorative.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic يَا (yā).
From Arabic يااللّٰه (yallā).

parole.significato: you win some, you lose some. There are good and bad days.
parole.testo: From Arabic يَوْم عَسَل وَيَوْم بَصَل (yawm ʕasal wayawm baṣal, literally “(one) day of honey, (one) day of onion”).

parole.significato: that is, in other words, meaning, like
parole.testo: From Arabic يَعْنِي (yaʕnī), third-person masculine singular of عَنَى (ʕanā, “to mean”), cognate to native עָנָה (aná, “to answer”) and יַעַן (yá'an, “since, because”).
Borrowed from Arabic كف.
Borrowed from Arabic كُسّ (kuss), from Classical Persian کُس (kus, “cunt”).
From Arabic كُفْتَة (kufta), from Persian کوفته (kufte).
Borrowed from Arabic قُطْن (quṭn, “cotton”), with the spelling being adjusted to Aramaic כִּתָּנָא (kitaná, “flax, linen”) and Hebrew כֻּתֹּנֶת (kutónet, “tunic”).

parole.significato: Ferula, A taxonomic genus within the family Apiaceae.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic كَلْخ (kalḵ), from the earlier قَلْح (qalḥ), itself from Classical Syriac ܩܠܚܠܚܐ (qlaḥlāḥā, “giant fennel”)/Aramaic קִלְחָא (qilḥā).
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda from כרוב (“cabbage”) + ־ית, under influence of Arabic قَرْنَبِيط (qarnabīṭ), which itself was derived from Ancient Greek κράμβη (krámbē, “cabbage”).
From Arabic لَفَّة (laffa).
Related to Arabic لَهَب (lahab, “flame”)

parole.significato: lahoh, a spongy, pancake-like bread originating in Djibouti, Somaliland, Somalia, and Yemen
parole.testo: From Arabic لَحُوح (laḥūḥ), popularized in Israel by Yemenite Jews.

parole.significato: A tune (as the tune of a song), a melody.
parole.testo: From Arabic لَحْن (laḥn). Attested since Medieval Hebrew, for example in the Kuzari.
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda in 1904, from Arabic لَطَّفَ (laṭṭafa)
From Arabic مَبْسُوط (mabsūṭ), passive participle of بَسَطَ (basaṭa).
Borrowed from Arabic مَبْرُوك (mabrūk, “congratulations”, interjection).
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda based upon Arabic بَرْقِيَّة (barqiyya). See בָּרָק (barák, “lightning”).
Borrowed from Arabic مَجْنُون (majnūn).
Borrowed from Arabic مُؤَذِّن (muʔaḏḏin), ultimately from a shared root, see Proto-Semitic *ʔuḏn- (“ear”).

parole.significato: to be barbecued or grilled on a mangal
parole.testo: Denominated from מַנְגָּל (“small portable grill”), from Arabic مِنْقَل (minqal, “brazier”). See מַנְגָּל.

parole.significato: Muslim: of or pertaining to Muslims, or being a Muslim or Muslims.
parole.testo: From Arabic مُسْلِم (muslim) + ־ִי (-í, “-ic, -an”); compare English Muslim.

parole.significato: a caffè mocha, a mochaccino, a mocha
parole.testo: Ultimately from Arabic اَلْمُخَا (al-muḵā). See mocha.
From Arabic مُشْط (mušṭ, literally “comb”), because of the shape of its tail.
Borrowed from Arabic مَكْتُوب (maktūb, “destined, ordained”).
Calque of Arabic مَسْجِد (masjid): formed in modern times by applying the pattern מִקְטָל (“place”) to סָגַד (sagád, “to bow down, prostrate”), which is cognate with Arabic سَجَدَ (sajada).

parole.significato: drugged, high, wasted, drunk (under the psychological effects of a mood-affecting drug)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic مَسْطُول (masṭūl, “intoxicated, drugged”).

parole.significato: A codex of the Bible (as a book rather than a scroll).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic مُصْحَف (muṣḥaf), borrowed from Ge'ez መጽሐፍ (mäṣḥäf), from ጸሐፈ (ṣäḥäfä).

parole.significato: A source, an origin, a root.
parole.testo: From קור (“to dig”). The sense “infinitive” is a possible semantic loan from Arabic مَصْدَر (maṣdar, “infinitive”, literally “source, origin”).
A medieval borrowing from Arabic مَرْكَز (markaz). According to Ben-Yehuda probably introduced by Abraham bar Hiyya.

parole.significato: apricot (a round sweet and juicy stone fruit, resembling peach or plum in taste, with a yellow-orange flesh, lightly fu…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic مِشْمِش (mišmiš, “apricots”).
Abbreviation of אבן (ibn, “the son of”), which is from Arabic اِبْن (ibn).
Post-biblical borrowing from Arabic نَاقَةٌ (nāqatun).

parole.significato: one of several repeated trips, rounds, or runs of an action
parole.testo: From dialectal Arabic نَقْلَة (naqla), singulative of نَقْل (naql, “transport or transfer of something”).
Borrowed from Arabic نَحْس (naḥs, “bad luck, ill omen”). Doublet of נַחַשׁ (nákhash, “sorcery”).
From Arabic صَبَابَة (ṣabāba).

Borrowed from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), borrowed from Middle Persian 𐭱𐭪𐭥 (šakar), borrowed from Gandhari 𐨭𐨐𐨪 (śakara), from Sanskrit शर्क॑रा (śárkarā), from Proto-Indo-Aryan *śárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárkaraH, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱorkeh₂ (“gravel”).
Borrowed from Arabic سُنِّيّ (sunniyy).
From Arabic صاحبك (ṣāḥbak, “your friend”).
Borrowed from Arabic سُنَّة (sunna).

Borrowed from Arabic عُود (ʕūd).
In the “consonant” sense, likely a mediaeval calque of Arabic مُتَحَرِّك (mutaḥarrik).
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda, from עיר ('ir) + ־ייה / ־ִיָּה (-iyá), by analogy with Arabic بَلَدِيَّة (baladiyya).
Borrowed from Arabic عَقْعَق (ʕaqʕaq).

parole.significato: a loud, low-class, uncultured young man, particularly if Sephardic; chav, douchebag.
parole.testo: From Arabic عَرْص (ʕarṣ, “pimp”).

parole.significato: arak (a clear, unsweetened aniseed-flavoured alcoholic drink, produced and consumed primarily in the Levant)
parole.testo: From Arabic عَرَق (ʕaraq).

parole.significato: an embarrassing, ridiculous or laughable situation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic فَضِيحَة (faḍīḥa).

parole.significato: pistachio (the nutlike fruit of this tree)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic فُسْتُق (fustuq), from Middle Persian pstk' (pistag).
Borrowed from Arabic فَنَّان (fannān, “artist”), from Arabic فَنّ (fann, “art, genre”), from Classical Persian پند (pand, “knack, trick”).
Borrowed from Arabic فَرْو (farw). Coined by Russian hebrew linguist, grammarian, journalist, lexicographer, newspaper editor and Zionist activist Eliezer Ben-Yehuda.
Borrowed from Arabic صَبَّار (ṣabbār).
Borrowed from Arabic صَدَف (ṣadaf).
Borrowed from Arabic صَلِيل (ṣalīl) during the medieval period.
Borrowed from Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa).
Coined by Judah ben Saul ibn Tibbon (c. 1120 – 1190 CE), from Arabic قُطْب (quṭb).

In Biblical Hebrew: Cognate to Arabic قُطْب (quṭb), and Classical Syriac ܩܘܽܪܛܒܳܐ (qurṭəḇā), ܛܘܽܪܛܒܳܐ (ṭurṭəḇā), ܩܘܽܛܒܳܐ (quṭəḇā), ܩܘܽܛܒܬܳܐ (quṭəḇtā, “puncture-vine”). For the formation compare قُرْط (qurṭ, “Egyptian clover”), قَتَاد (qatād, “milkvetch”), قَتّ (qatt, “lucerne”), قَات (qāt, “qat”), ق
From Arabic قُطْر (quṭr).
From Arabic قَطِيفَة (qaṭīfa).
From Arabic قَسَّام (qassām).

parole.significato: jam (sweet mixture of fruit boiled with sugar)
parole.testo: Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda. A combination of the Hebrew root רבב and Arabic مُرَبَّى (murabbā, “jam, marmalade”), رُبّ (rubb, “pulp”) and رَوْب (rawb, “stiffened milk”).
Borrowed from Arabic رَيْحَان (rayḥān).
Coined by Eliezer Ben-Yehuda based upon Arabic رَسْمِيّ (rasmiyy). From רֹשֶׁם (róshem, “impression”) + ־י (-í); compare Assyrian Neo-Aramaic ܪܘܼܫܡܵܝܵܐ (rušmāyā).
Borrowed from Arabic شَدَّة (šadda).
Borrowed from Arabic شَيْخ (šayḵ).
Arabic شِيعِيّ (šīʕiyy). Cognate with Hebrew סיעה.
Borrowed from Arabic سُلَحْفَاة (sulaḥfāh), ultimately from Akkadian 𒃻𒅮𒈾 (šeleppûm). Compare Aramaic ܣܠܘܦܝܬܐ (sallōp̄īṯā).

Coined by Israeli poet Avraham Shlonsky, a prolific creator of Modern Hebrew neologisms. Learned borrowing from Arabic سَمَك (samak, “fish”), ultimately from the root س م ك (s m k), meaning "to be held up, supported" and "to sustain", from which its meaning of "source of sustenance" was derived. parole.significato: shakshuka (dish of eggs simmered in a mixture of vegetables and spices)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Arabic شَكْشُوكَة (šakšūka).
Borrowed from Arabic شَرِيف (šarīf).
Borrowed from Arabic شَرْمُوطَة (šarmūṭa).
Borrowed from Arabic تَأْرِيخ (taʔrīḵ, “date”). Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *warḫ-.

Borrowed from Arabic تمساح, itself from Coptic ⲙⲥⲁϩ (msah), from Egyptian G17-O34:V28-I3 mzḥ (“crocodile”). Perhaps with the singular feminine definite article ⲧⲉ- (te-), though ⲙⲥⲁϩ (msah) is a masculine word.
Borrowed from Arabic تَمْرِين (tamrīn). Coined by Russian hebrew linguist, grammarian, journalist, lexicographer, newspaper editor and Zionist activist Eliezer Ben-Yehuda.
From Arabic تَنْوِين (tanwīn)
In the “vowel” sense, likely a mediaeval calque of Arabic حَرَكَة (ḥaraka).
